Ballet is a formalized system of theatrical dance that originated in Renaissance Italy and developed into its classical form in France and Russia during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Defined by turned-out legs, vertical alignment, precise arm positions, and ethereal lightness, ballet became the preeminent vehicle for storytelling through movement in the Western tradition. It remains the foundation upon which most Western concert dance rests.

Ballet emerged in Italian Renaissance courts as an entertainment combining music, dance, and spectacle. The term comes from the Italian word balletto, meaning a dancing figure. It was King Louis the Fourteenth of France, himself a dancer, who truly systematized the art form. In sixteen sixty-one, he established the Académie Royale de Danse, which systematized ballet technique and terminology. This codification during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries transformed ballet from court entertainment into a formal theatrical spectacle. The Baroque composers like Jean Philippe Rameau created ballet works that were early operas-ballets, expanding the form's artistic scope.

The five positions of the feet are the foundational stances in which the dancer's feet are arranged, with heels together or apart and toes turned out at ninety degrees. These positions form the grammar of ballet and have remained unchanged for three hundred and fifty years. The port de bras, the arm positions, are equally codified and essential.

The Romantic era of the eighteen thirties through eighteen seventies transformed ballet's emotional character and visual aesthetic. Works like La Sylphide and Giselle emphasized supernatural, ethereal imagery and emotional intensity. Dancers wore white tutus and danced en pointe, on the tips of their toes in special shoes, creating an illusion of weightlessness and otherworldliness that captivated audiences.

Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky elevated ballet to the highest artistic level. His masterworks—Swan Lake, The Nutcracker, and Sleeping Beauty—combined symphonic orchestration with profound emotional and narrative depth, giving ballet works the status of concert music. The Russian Imperial Ballet, centered in St. Petersburg and Moscow during the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, produced the great choreographer Marius Petipa, who created the classical vocabulary that defined the canon.

The early twentieth century brought radical innovation. Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, operating from nineteen oh nine to nineteen twenty-nine, was a revolutionary company that challenged convention. He commissioned Igor Stravinsky to write The Firebird and The Rite of Spring, two masterworks that bridged Romantic and modernist ballet. Diaghilev collaborated with visual artists like Picasso and Matisse and revolutionary choreographers like Vaslav Nijinsky. George Balanchine, who lived from nineteen oh four to nineteen eighty-three, created neoclassical ballet, stripping away narrative and emphasizing pure movement and music. His works dominate the modern ballet repertoire and remain central to the art form today.
